controls.statement: Maintain an inventory of personal and sensitive data.
Record the source, purpose, lawful basis or authorization, recipients, location, retention, and deletion method for each category.
Collect only data necessary for the documented purpose.
Privacy-protective defaults are used.
Product behavior matches the published privacy notice.
New data uses have undergone privacy review.
Consent is used only where appropriate.
Consent is specific, informed, granular, recorded, and withdrawable.
Refusing nonessential consent does not improperly block the service.
Nonessential trackers are prevented from operating before valid permission where required.
Cookie and tracker inventories match actual production behavior.
Analytics, advertising, attribution, session replay, and experimentation tools receive only approved data.
Sensitive fields are redacted from logs, monitoring, support tools, recordings, and analytics.
Access, correction, deletion, restriction, objection, and portability workflows exist where applicable.
Rights requests cover downstream systems and processors.
Requester identity verification is proportionate and does not collect excessive additional data.
Rights-response deadlines are tracked.
Retention periods are explicit.
Deletion occurs across primary data, caches, indexes, derived data, and downstream systems.
Backup deletion behavior is documented and legally acceptable.
Legal holds override deletion only through a controlled process.
Pseudonymization or anonymization claims have been validated.
Reidentification risk has been assessed.
Data export does not expose other users’ or tenants’ information.
High-risk processing has an appropriate privacy-impact assessment.
Children’s, biometric, health, precise-location, communications, financial, and other sensitive data trigger enhanced review.
Cross-border transfers and data-residency commitments are documented.
Processor and subprocessor contracts cover permitted use, security, deletion, assistance, and breach notification.
Privacy contacts and escalation paths exist.
A personal-data incident can be identified, scoped, and reported within applicable deadlines.
Production support access to personal data is minimized and audited.
Synthetic or masked data is used outside production.
Test accounts and deleted users do not remain indefinitely in downstream tools.
Interfaces avoid manipulative consent, cancellation, or privacy choices.
Performance objectives are defined per critical user journey.
Objectives use relevant percentiles, not averages alone.
Frontend and backend budgets are documented.
Baseline performance is recorded before launch.
Laboratory tests and real-user measurements are both used where applicable.
Public pages meet approved loading, interaction, and visual-stability targets.
API latency targets are defined per endpoint or journey.
Database-query latency and volume are measured.
Excessive query patterns and repeated fetches have been eliminated.
Payload sizes are bounded.
Compression is enabled appropriately.
Images, fonts, scripts, and styles are delivered efficiently.
Critical resources are prioritized.
Noncritical work is deferred without harming accessibility or correctness.
Cache and CDN behavior has been validated.
Cold-start performance is acceptable.
Connection and thread pools are sized and monitored.
Memory, CPU, file-descriptor, connection, and storage leaks have been investigated.
Long-running or resource-intensive requests have limits.
Performance is tested with realistic authentication, authorization, data volume, and cache state.
Performance is tested on representative mobile devices and slower networks where relevant.
Third-party script and service impact is measured.
Performance degradation during partial dependency failure is acceptable.
Performance regressions have automated release thresholds.
Client telemetry does not itself materially harm performance.
Performance objectives are connected to user and business outcomes.
Forecast normal, peak, burst, launch, seasonal, and abuse traffic.
Forecast data, file, index, queue, log, and backup growth.
Identify the maximum safe capacity of each critical component.
Load tests use realistic request mixes and data distributions.
Load tests include authentication and authorization overhead.
Load tests include external dependency behavior.
Stress testing identifies how the system fails beyond capacity.
Spike testing covers sudden surges.
Endurance testing identifies leaks and gradual degradation.
Capacity testing includes the largest expected tenant or customer.
Provider quotas and account limits have been reviewed.
Database connections, locks, storage, replicas, and I/O have sufficient headroom.
Queue, cache, load-balancer, network, and worker capacity have sufficient headroom.
Autoscaling minimums, maximums, triggers, cooldowns, and scale-down behavior are validated.
Scaling does not overload a database or dependency.
Capacity remains sufficient during a zone, node, or region failure according to the design.
Rate limits protect shared capacity fairly.
Per-user and per-tenant quotas prevent noisy-neighbor failure.
Backpressure propagates safely.
Queues are bounded or have explicit overload behavior.
Load shedding preserves the most important operations.
Retry storms are prevented.
Expensive optional functionality can degrade or disable safely.
DDoS scenarios and provider protections have been reviewed.
Capacity-related alert thresholds provide enough time to act.
The cost of expected and peak operation has been modeled.
Cost limits do not silently terminate essential operation.
Capacity assumptions have owners and review dates.
